power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.51", "p=0.49", "p=0.30", "p=0.67", "p≥0.32", "p≥0.10"), Sentence = c("The associations with partnership quality (p=0.51), research engagement (p=0.49), trust in medical researchers (p=0.30), and partnership recommendation (p=0.67) did not differ by race.", "The associations with partnership quality (p=0.51), research engagement (p=0.49), trust in medical researchers (p=0.30), and partnership recommendation (p=0.67) did not differ by race.", "The associations with partnership quality (p=0.51), research engagement (p=0.49), trust in medical researchers (p=0.30), and partnership recommendation (p=0.67) did not differ by race.", "The associations with partnership quality (p=0.51), research engagement (p=0.49), trust in medical researchers (p=0.30), and partnership recommendation (p=0.67) did not differ by race.", "In contrast, no statistically significant associations were observed for study design (all p≥0.32) or community advisory board (all p≥0.10) contributions with any outcome.", "In contrast, no statistically significant associations were observed for study design (all p≥0.32) or community advisory board (all p≥0.10) contributions with any outcome." )), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Is greater patient involvement in patient-centered outcomes research associated with partnership quality, research engagement, trust in medical researchers, and partnership recommendation?

This national cohort study found that patient research involvement was significantly associated with all four primary outcomes and that these associations were primarily driven by patient partners' participation in recruitment, grant writing, data collection, and shared governance.

Patient-centered outcomes research involvement across the research process may improve partnership quality, indicating the importance of patient and community partnership in shared decision-making and roles creating visible impact.

Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s): Primary outcomes included partnership quality and research engagement, with trust in medical researchers and partnership recommendation as secondary and tertiary outcomes.
Multivariable linear and modified Poisson regressions were utilized to estimate regression coefficients and adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs).
Results: Among 330 participants (mean age = 36.5 years, SD = 9.7), 56.1% were male, and 37.3% and 31.8% were White or Black, respectively.

Involvement in patient-centered outcomes research was associated with partnership quality (β, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.30-1.42, P=0.003), research engagement (β, 0.04; 95% CI, 0.01-0.06, P=0.006), trust in medical researchers (β, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.31-1.07, P<0.001), and greater willingness to recommend becoming a research partner (aPR, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.05-1.14, P<0.001).

text.text: Patient-centered outcomes research may provide patient and community research partners with a sense of shared ownership, improving partnership quality.
While the causal links require further investigation, these associations may be driven by inclusion in recruitment, grant writing, data collection, and shared governance.

Patient-centered outcomes research offers patients and community members a pathway to offer their lived experience expertise to shape research projects. 1 Patient and community involvement in such research can span the entire research process, from ideation and grant writing to defining research questions, identifying meaningful outcomes, interpreting findings, and disseminating results. 2, 3 Patient-centered outcomes research may increase representation of underserved populations in research, 4, 5 improve research engagement and partnership quality, 6 and align decision-making with patients' perspectives and experiences. 7 Engaging patients and communities as partners in research has been linked to more relevant interventions and better uptake of findings in the real world beyond clinical settings, 8, 9 which could shorten the gap between developing an intervention and adopting it into practice. 10, 11 Evidence for these benefits, however, remains limited.

text.text: Understanding these associations is needed for identifying appropriate engagement strategies that support high-quality partnerships, build trust, and sustain meaningful stakeholder engagement throughout the research process.
This study examined the associations of research involvement with the outcomes of patient and community partnerships.

Using data from a national cohort of patient and community research partners (N = 330), we examined whether greater research involvement was associated with (1) partnership quality, (2) research engagement, (3) trust in medical researchers, and (4) willingness to recommend being a research partner.
We additionally explored whether specific types of research involvement, such as study design, recruitment, and shared governance, were differentially associated with these outcomes.
This cross-sectional study used baseline data from a cohort study of patient and community research partners in the United States.
Data were primarily collected to validate the Quality of Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Partnerships (QPCOR) instrument, 17 and this analysis represents a secondary use of that data.

Eligible participants were asked to complete an online survey administered at study enrollment and at three-and six-month follow-up engagements, though this analysis is restricted to baseline data collected at study enrollment.
Secondary measures included research involvement and engagement, trust in medical researchers, willingness to recommend becoming a research partner, and sociodemographic factors.
A total of 330 participants enrolled between September and December 2024.

Participants could select all that applied from the following responses: (1) study design, (2) recruitment, (3) retention management, (4) data interpretation, (5) dissemination, (6) grant writing, (7) community advisory board, (8) data collection, (9) shared governance, and (10) other.
A composite measure (primary exposure) was constructed as the sum of checked responses.

Regarding research involvement, participants contributed to approximately three research activities on average (mean = 2.6, SD = 2.5).
The highest involvement was in recruitment (43.6%), followed by data collection (36.7%), dissemination (32.7%), and data interpretation (29.1%).

On average, participants reported high partnership quality (mean = 86.7, SD = 12.6), high research engagement (mean = 4.3, SD = 0.5), and moderate trust in medical researchers (mean = 28.2, SD = 8.1).
Forty-five percent indicated that they would highly recommend being a research partner.

Other statistically significant relationships included data interpretation with trust in medical researchers (β = 2.05, 95% CI: 0.08 to 4.02) and partnership recommendation (aPR = 1.33, 95% CI: 1.02 to 1.71), and retention management with trust in medical researchers (β = 2.36, 95% CI: 0.13 to 4.58).
In contrast, no statistically significant associations were observed for study design (all p≥0.32) or community advisory board (all p≥0.10) contributions with any outcome.

Increased research involvement was significantly associated with improved patient and community partnerships (i.e., partnership quality, research engagement, trust in medical researchers, and partnership recommendation).
Importantly, these outcomes did not differ by race.

The association with trust in medical researchers is particularly relevant given that confidence in scientists to act in the public's best interests has declined among U.S. adults, from approximately 87% in 2020 to 76% in 2024. 32 This is consistent with the present study's findings, in which trust emerges from sustained partnership instead of episodic consultation, 33 suggesting that greater involvement may help build trust in patients and communities where mistrust of research institutions has historically limited participation. 34 These outcomes were associated with being a patient or community partner as well as the extent of these partnerships.

Notably, participation on a community advisory board was not associated with any of the examined outcomes; however, shared governance was associated with each outcome.

While community advisory boards are useful, they often face challenges in recruitment, trust, and retention 35, 36 and may be viewed as tokenistic. 37 They nonetheless remain among the most common structures for engaging communities in research, 38 a prevalence that may reflect longstanding funder expectations 39 and the relative ease of convening an advisory group within short timelines.This implies that the value of advisory structures may not depend solely on their existence, but on the quality of engagement they enable. 40 Patient-centered research may benefit from enhancing shared governance in research as a means for patient and community engagement.

text.text: Shared governance structures may therefore be associated with improved partnerships and offer a more sustainable approach.
Beyond governance-related activities, involvement in recruitment and data collection was also associated with improved partnership outcomes.
These activities may provide patients and communities with direct opportunities to utilize their lived experiences and observe their contributions' impact.

Such visibility may reinforce partners' sense of shared ownership of the research process, suggesting that meaningful engagement includes ensuring that partners' roles involve substantive contributions to study implementation.
Together, these findings demonstrate the need for meaningful patient and community engagement throughout the research process.
Many types of research involvement that were associated with individual outcomes were also associated with all four outcomes.
While these outcomes each measure different aspects of patient and community partnerships, they may be related and reinforce one another.
This study's cross-sectional nature enables limited causal inference.

Participants more involved in research may perceive increased partnership quality, trust, and engagement; however, individuals who already have more positive perceptions of research may also be more likely to pursue greater research involvement.
Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify whether increased research involvement precedes improved partnership outcomes.
Additionally, this study consisted of patient and community partners.
Therefore, this study may not be generalizable to individuals who have not participated in research partnerships.
Finally, all measures were self-reported and may be subject to social desirability bias.
Still, this study is among the first to examine how research involvement is associated with the quality of partnerships with patients and community members.
In this national study of patient and community research partners, the extent of partners' involvement in research was significantly associated with improved partnership outcomes.
Notably, not all forms of research involvement are associated with the same outcomes.

Roles involving equal decision-making authority or those that create more visible impact for patient partners, such as shared governance, grant writing, recruitment, and data collection, were consistently associated with improved partnership outcomes.
In contrast, such associations were not observed for consultative roles, such as community advisory boards.

These findings suggest that future patient-centered outcomes research should involve patient and community partners throughout the research process and focus on active roles that foster shared ownership between researchers and community partners.

Still, little is known about the extent to which greater patient involvement in research partnerships is associated with higher partnership quality, greater research engagement, increased trust in medical researchers, and a greater willingness to recommend serving as a research partner.

Greater research involvement was significantly associated with higher partnership quality, greater research engagement, increased trust in medical researchers, and stronger partnership recommendation in a national sample of U.S. patient and community research partners.
Secondary analyses suggested that these associations may be driven by contributions to recruitment, grant writing, data collection, and shared governance.
By contrast, contributions to study design and community advisory boards showed no statistically significant associations with any of the four outcomes.
Together, these findings point to potential links between research involvement and community-engaged research outcomes, warranting longitudinal evaluation of the underlying causal pathways.
